hmmt-feb-1998-calc-01.title: Maximise the distance
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-01.body:
Read the paths as the official solution does: when Tim has walked $t$ minutes, Alex has walked $m=t-5$ minutes, so Tim is at $(t,\sin t)$ and Alex is at $(t-5,\cos t)$. The squared distance is
$$d^2=25+(\sin t-\cos t)^2 .$$
Now $(\sin t-\cos t)^2=1-\sin2t$ takes its largest value $2$ (when $\sin 2t=-1$, e.g. $t=\frac{3\pi}4+2\pi k$ with $t\ge5$). Hence $d_{\max}^2=25+2=27$ and $d_{\max}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-02.title: Equate volume flow
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-02.body:
Water leaves the cube at $(1\ \text{m}^2)(1\ \text{cm/s})=1\ \text{cm}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$. It enters the cylinder at $\pi r^2\frac{dh}{dt}=\pi\cdot1\ \text{m}^2\cdot\frac{dh}{dt}$. Setting these equal gives $\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac1\pi$ cm/s.

**Answer: $\frac1\pi$ cm/s**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-03.title: Two pieces
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-03.body:
The curves $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ meet at $x=0$ and $x=1$. On $[0,1]$ the line is above the parabola; on $[1,2]$ the parabola is above the line, so the bounded region (closed off by $x=2$) has area
$$\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx+\int_1^2(x^2-x)\,dx=\frac16+\frac56=1.$$

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-04.title: Sum the series
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-04.body:
$f$ is a geometric series with ratio $\frac x2$, so $f(x)=\frac1{1-x/2}=\frac2{2-x}$. Then $\int_0^1\frac2{2-x}dx=\bigl[-2\ln(2-x)\bigr]_0^1=2\ln2$. Hence $\sqrt{e^{2\ln2}}=\sqrt4=2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-05.title: Take logarithms
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-05.body:
Write $x^{x/\sin(1-x)}=\exp\!\left(\frac{x\ln x}{\sin(1-x)}\right)$. As $x\to1$ the exponent is of the form $\frac00$. By L'Hopital's rule
$$\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x\ln x}{\sin(1-x)}=\lim_{x\to1}\frac{\ln x+1}{-\cos(1-x)}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.$$
So the limit is $e^{-1}$.

**Answer: $\frac1e$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-06.title: Positions as functions of time
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-06.body:
After $t$ seconds Edward is $1875+\frac12t^2$ feet from the prison and the arrow is $100t-\frac12t^2$ feet away. They meet when $1875+\frac12t^2=100t-\frac12t^2$, i.e. $t^2-100t+1875=0$, so $t=25$ or $t=75$. The arrow hits Edward the first time, at $t=25$ (afterwards he is no longer in front of it). The arrow's speed is then $100-25\cdot1=75$ ft/s.

**Answer: 75 ft/s**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-07.title: Find the parabola
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-07.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. The parabola passes through $A$ and $B$ with tangent slopes $\sqrt3$ at $A$ and $-\sqrt3$ at $B$ (the slopes of $AC$ and $BC$). With $y=ax^2+bx+c$: $c=0$, $b=\sqrt3$, $2a+b=-\sqrt3$ so $a=-\sqrt3$. Thus $y=\sqrt3(x-x^2)$.

The area between $AB$ and the parabola is $\int_0^1\sqrt3(x-x^2)\,dx=\sqrt3\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}6$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}6$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-08.title: Tangency conditions
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-08.body:
A line $y=mx$ through the origin is tangent at a point $(x,y)$ with $y=mx$ and slope $m=\frac{dy}{dx}$. Differentiating, $2y\,y'=3x^2+39$, so $m=\frac{3x^2+39}{2mx}$, i.e. $2m^2x=3x^2+39$. Also $m^2x^2=x^3+39x-35$.

Eliminating $m^2=\frac{x^3+39x-35}{x^2}$: $\frac{2(x^3+39x-35)}{x}=3x^2+39$, so $x^3-39x+70=0$, i.e. $(x-2)(x-5)(x+7)=0$.

- $x=2$: $m^2=\frac{8+78-35}{4}=\frac{51}4$, $m=\pm\frac{\sqrt{51}}2$.
- $x=5$: $m^2=\frac{125+195-35}{25}=\frac{285}{25}$, $m=\pm\frac{\sqrt{285}}5$.
- $x=-7$: $x^3+39x-35<0$, so no real point.

**Answer: $\pm\frac{\sqrt{51}}2,\ \pm\frac{\sqrt{285}}5$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-09.title: Integrate the series from problem 4
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-09.body:
$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^{n-1}}{2^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{1-x/2}$, and integrating term by term from $0$ to $1$ gives $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n\,2^{n-1}}=\int_0^1\frac{2}{2-x}dx=2\ln2$.

**Answer: $2\ln2$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-09.title: Logarithm series
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-09.body:
$-\ln(1-u)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{u^n}n$. With $u=\frac12$: $\ln2=\sum\frac1{n2^n}$, so the given sum is $2\ln2$.

**Answer: $2\ln 2$**

hmmt-feb-1998-calc-10.title: Quadratic in $t$
hmmt-feb-1998-calc-10.body:
Clearing denominators: $x(1-t)+yt=t(1-t)$, i.e. $g(t)=t^2+(y-x-1)t+x=0$. For $x,y>0$ we have $g(0)=x>0$ and $g(1)=y>0$, so a root in $(0,1)$ exists iff there are two real roots and the vertex $t=\frac{1+x-y}2$ lies in $(0,1)$.

Real roots need $(y-x-1)^2\ge4x$, i.e. $y\ge x+1+2\sqrt x$ or $y\le x+1-2\sqrt x=(1-\sqrt x)^2$. The first option violates $y<1+x$ (vertex condition), and the second forces $x<1$ (for $x\ge1$, $y\le(\sqrt x-1)^2<x-1$ contradicts $y>x-1$). So $S=\{0<x<1,\ 0<y\le(1-\sqrt x)^2\}$ and
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^1\left(x+1-2\sqrt x\right)dx=\frac12+1-\frac43=\frac16.$$

**Answer: $\frac16$**
